## Solution

**Substitution.** Let $u = x/n$, so $x = nu$, $dx = n\,du$. The limits $x:0\to n$ become $u:0\to 1$:
$$I_n := \int_0^n (1+x/n)^{-n}\log(2+\cos(x/n))\,dx = n\int_0^1 (1+u)^{-n}\log(2+\cos u)\,du.$$

**Rescale near the concentration point.** The factor $(1+u)^{-n}=e^{-n\log(1+u)}$ decays exponentially for $u>0$ and equals $1$ at $u=0$, so the mass concentrates near $u=0$. Set $t = nu$ (i.e. $u = t/n$, $du = dt/n$); the limits become $t:0\to n$:
$$I_n = \int_0^n e^{-n\log(1+t/n)}\,\log\!\bigl(2+\cos(t/n)\bigr)\,dt.$$

**Pointwise limit of the integrand.** For each fixed $t\ge 0$:
- $n\log(1+t/n) \to t$, so $e^{-n\log(1+t/n)}\to e^{-t}$;
- $\cos(t/n)\to 1$, so $\log(2+\cos(t/n))\to \log 3$.

Hence the integrand converges pointwise to $e^{-t}\log 3$.

**Dominating function (for $0\le t\le n$).** Use the standard inequality $\log(1+s)\ge \dfrac{s}{1+s}$ for $s\ge 0$ with $s=t/n$:
$$n\log(1+t/n)\ge \frac{nt}{n+t}.$$
For $0\le t\le n$ we have $n+t\le 2n$, hence $n\log(1+t/n)\ge t/2$, giving
$$e^{-n\log(1+t/n)}\le e^{-t/2}.$$
Also $2+\cos(t/n)\in[1,3]$, so $0\le \log(2+\cos(t/n))\le \log 3$. Therefore the integrand is bounded by
$$\bigl|e^{-n\log(1+t/n)}\log(2+\cos(t/n))\bigr|\le (\log 3)\,e^{-t/2},\qquad 0\le t\le n,$$
and $(\log 3)\,e^{-t/2}$ is integrable on $[0,\infty)$.

**Apply dominated convergence.** Extending the integrand by $0$ for $t>n$, dominated convergence yields
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} I_n = \int_0^\infty e^{-t}\log 3\,dt = \log 3\cdot\int_0^\infty e^{-t}\,dt = \log 3.$$

$$\boxed{\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^n (1+x/n)^{-n}\log(2+\cos(x/n))\,dx = \log 3.}$$
